Get started with zupmxode

zupmxode.Rmd
library(zupmxode)

rxode2 and mrgsolve compile every model with the system C compiler, which locked-down and validated machines often lack. zupmxode runs the same models with nothing but R. This page compiles a one-compartment model with first-order absorption, and gives it a week of daily 100 mg doses:

ev <- zupmxode_events(amt = 100, ii = 24, addl = 6, cmt = "depot",
                      time = seq(0, 168, by = 1))

Compile a model

The model is written in rxode2’s syntax and read by R’s own parser, so existing rxode2 models run unchanged. It is compiled to native code in milliseconds, without a compiler.

# Open: Q6, should the R functions be pmx_ode_*() rather than zupmxode_*()?
m <- zupmxode_model({
  ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka); cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl); v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
  d/dt(depot)   <- -ka * depot
  d/dt(central) <-  ka * depot - cl / v * central
  cp <- central / v
})
zupmxode_info(m)

Solve one subject

zupmxode_solve() is the deterministic core: parameters in, predictions out, with no random draws.

out <- zupmxode_solve(m, ev, params = c(tka = 0.5, tcl = 1, tv = 3,
                                        eta.ka = 0, eta.cl = 0,
                                        eta.v = 0))

Simulate a population, reproducibly

Between-subject variability and residual error are drawn in R with R’s random number generator, and the C engine stays deterministic. The same seed gives the same result at any thread count.

zupmxode_threads(8)
set.seed(1)
sim <- zupmxode_sim(m, ev, theta = c(tka = 0.5, tcl = 1, tv = 3),
                    omega = diag(c(0.1, 0.1, 0.1)),
                    sigma = list(cp = prop(0.1)), n = 1000)

Choose the solver and the tier

The solver is the most specific one the model allows (closed form, matrix exponential, or a general ODE solver), and the tier is native code unless the platform cannot run it. zupmxode_info() says which was chosen, and both can be overridden.

zupmxode_method(m, "lsoda")
zupmxode_tier(m, "interp")
